claims.text: Engineered coherent nanoprecipitates can be introduced into a tungsten-based refractory alloy.
Coherent nanoprecipitates relieve stress concentrations that could cause premature crack initiation.
Coherent nanoprecipitates promote dislocation climb at temperatures above 0.5 Tm.
The nanoprecipitates provide localized stress concentrations that facilitate dislocation climb.
Nanoprecipitate-enabled dislocation transmission and stress redistribution allow additional plastic deformation without premature crack initiation.
Coherent nanoprecipitates improve high-temperature plastic strain relative to an unmodified refractory-alloy baseline.
Coherent nanoprecipitates improve high-temperature fracture toughness relative to an unmodified refractory-alloy baseline.
The same nanoprecipitate-mediated dislocation mechanism simultaneously enhances high-temperature plastic strain and fracture toughness.
The hypothesis applies to homogeneous refractory alloys at temperatures above 0.5 Tm and at strain rates relevant to fusion-reactor service.
The proposed mechanism may not apply below 0.5 Tm.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in microstructures with significant heterogeneity or impurity segregation.
Nanoprecipitate size, density, and distribution affect the magnitude of the ductility and toughness response.
The mechanical response is sensitive to alloy composition.
High-temperature dislocation behavior is sensitive to test strain rate.

contradictions.description: The nanoprecipitates are described as stress relievers in the structural mediator field but as sources of localized stress concentrations in the mechanism field, without distinguishing interface-scale stress localization from net stress relief.

The baseline is required to have identical alloy composition, but the intervention and experimental design permit introduction of precipitates through an alloying protocol, which could change composition unless both groups begin with the same composition and differ only in heat treatment or precipitate state.
